title: Genitive Case — Negation & Possession
explanation: The genitive case (dopełniacz) is used after negation (nie + verb), to express possession (belonging), and after certain prepositions like 'z' (from/with) and 'do' (to/into). When negating a verb that would normally take the accusative, the direct object switches to the genitive. Masculine animate genitive: -a (kot → kota). Masculine inanimate: -u or -a. Feminine: -y or -i (kawa → kawy). Neuter: -a (okno → okna).

examples.note: negation switches accusative to genitive: pies → psa

exercises.prompt: Which sentence correctly expresses 'I don't have a cat' (kot = cat, masculine animate)?
exercises.explanation: After negation with 'nie', the object shifts from accusative to genitive. Masculine animate genitive of 'kot' is 'kota'.

exercises.prompt: Complete: 'I don't have coffee.' (kawa = coffee, feminine — genitive: kawy)
exercises.explanation: Feminine nouns form the genitive by changing -a to -y (or -i after soft consonants): kawa → kawy.

exercises.prompt: How do you express possession: 'This is Piotr's house' (dom = house)?
exercises.explanation: Possession is expressed with the genitive. Male name 'Piotr' forms genitive as 'Piotra'. The owned item precedes the owner's name in genitive.

exercises.prompt: Complete: 'I am from Poland.' (Polska → Polski in genitive)
exercises.explanation: The preposition 'z' (from) requires the genitive case. 'Polska' (Poland) → 'Polski' in the genitive.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence uses the genitive correctly?
exercises.explanation: 'Mleko' (milk) is neuter. Genitive of neuter nouns ending in -o is formed by changing -o to -a: mleko → mleka. 'Nie ma' (there is no / he/she doesn't have) always takes the genitive.

exercises.prompt: Complete: 'I don't have time.' (czas = time, masculine inanimate — genitive: czasu)
exercises.explanation: Masculine inanimate nouns often form the genitive with -u: czas → czasu. Negation requires the genitive.
